    Group Theory

    Introduction

    Group theory primarily studies the algebraic structure of groups.

    To study the structure of groups, we need to master some basic tools, which include subgroups, group homomorphisms, and group actions. In competitive programming, the main groups involved are number-theoretic groups (such as the multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑛n, (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)×) and permutation groups. This article will focus on related concepts. Parts of group theory not covered in this article, such as the structure theory of finite groups and the linear representation theory of groups, should be referred to in specialized textbooks for interested readers.

    Notation

    When there is no ambiguity, this article may write 𝑔 ⋅ℎg⋅h as 𝑔ℎgh, and may also write the group (𝐺, ⋅)(G,⋅) as the group 𝐺G.

    Understanding abstract algebra cannot be separated from examples. As an example to understand the concepts below, here we discuss the spatial symmetry group 𝐷6D6 of an equilateral triangle.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle

    As shown in the figure, for a given equilateral triangle, there are six different operations that can make it coincide with itself.

    Here, 𝑟r is used to represent clockwise rotation, and 𝑠s represents reflection along the line from vertex 1 to the center of the triangle. Operations are composed from right to left, i.e., 𝑠𝑟sr means first rotate (𝑟r) then reflect (𝑠s). Two operations are different if and only if after the two operations, some vertex of the triangle is in a different position.

    SymbolOperationOrderPermutation Representation
    𝑒eIdentity transformation, i.e., do nothing1(1)(1)
    𝑟rClockwise rotation by 120∘120∘3(123)(123)
    𝑟2r2Clockwise rotation by 240∘240∘3(132)(132)
    𝑠sReflect along the line from vertex 1 to center2(23)(23)
    𝑠𝑟srFirst rotate 120∘120∘, then reflect2(13)(13)
    𝑠𝑟2sr2First rotate 240∘240∘, then reflect2(12)(12)

    It is easy to verify that these operations indeed form a group. For example, the identity element of this group is 𝑒e, and the inverse element of 𝑠𝑟sr is itself. Moreover, the group 𝐷6D6 is not abelian, for example, we can directly verify 𝑟𝑠 =𝑠𝑟−1rs=sr−1.

    The operations recorded in the table are not the only symmetric operations corresponding to those symbols. For example, "reflect along the line from vertex 2 to the center" is also a symmetric operation of the triangle. It is not in the table, but its result is the same as the operation "first rotate 120∘120∘, then reflect". Concepts such as "order" and "permutation representation" in the table will be explained below.

    Subgroups

    To understand the structure of a given group, we can first analyze its substructures. The substructure of a group is a subset of that group that still forms a group under the same operation. From this, we have the following definition.

    Subgroup

    For a group (𝐺, ⋅)(G,⋅) and its subset 𝐻 ⊆𝐺H⊆G, if (𝐻, ⋅)(H,⋅) is also a group, then the subset 𝐻H is called a subgroup of 𝐺G, denoted 𝐻 ≤𝐺H≤G.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    In 𝐷6D6, it is easy to verify that it has subgroups {𝑒}{e}, {𝑒,𝑠}{e,s}, {𝑒,𝑠𝑟}{e,sr}, {𝑒,𝑠𝑟2}{e,sr2}, {𝑒,𝑟,𝑟2}{e,r,r2}, and 𝐷6D6 itself, for a total of six. Except for 𝐷6D6 itself, the structures of these subgroups are simpler and contain some information about the original group.

    To determine whether a given subset 𝐻 ⊆𝐺H⊆G is a subgroup, we do not need to verify the group definition one by one: associativity naturally holds; for a subset to be a subgroup, we just need to ensure it is closed under the binary operation, has an identity element, and is closed under taking inverses. In fact, these conditions can be summarized together.

    Theorem (Subgroup Criterion)

    A subset 𝐻H of group 𝐺G is a subgroup if and only if for all elements 𝑔,ℎ ∈𝐻g,h∈H, we have 𝑔−1ℎ ∈𝐻g−1h∈H.

    Subgroups Generated by Subsets

    In general, given a subset 𝑆S in a group 𝐺G, starting from elements in 𝑆S, by repeatedly performing multiplication and taking inverses finite times, the set of all results obtained becomes a subgroup of 𝐺G. This is called the subgroup generated by the subset 𝑆S.

    Subgroup Generated by a Subset

    For a group 𝐺G and its non-empty subset 𝑆 ⊆𝐺S⊆G, if 𝐻H is the smallest subgroup of 𝐺G containing 𝑆S (with respect to inclusion), then 𝐻H is called the subgroup generated by a subset 𝑆S, denoted ⟨𝑆⟩⟨S⟩. Particularly, if 𝑆 ={𝑥}S={x} is a singleton, then ⟨𝑆⟩⟨S⟩ is also denoted ⟨𝑥⟩⟨x⟩, called the cyclic subgroup of the powers of 𝑥x.

    It can be proven that for any such subset 𝑆S, such a subgroup always exists: ⟨𝑆⟩⟨S⟩ can be constructed as the intersection of all subgroups of 𝐺G containing 𝑆S.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    In group 𝐷6D6, by selecting the rotation operation 𝑟r and repeatedly applying it and its inverse, we get the subgroup {𝑒,𝑟,𝑟2}{e,r,r2}. It can be denoted ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩. All non-trivial subgroups in group 𝐷6D6 can be generated by selecting some operation.

    Some subsets generate the entire group. Such subsets are particularly special and are called generating sets of the group.

    Generating Set of a Group

    If a subset 𝑆 ⊆𝐺S⊆G of group (𝐺, ⋅)(G,⋅) satisfies ⟨𝑆⟩ =𝐺⟨S⟩=G, then 𝑆S is called a generating set of the group 𝐺G. Elements in the generating set 𝑆S are called generators.

    The group itself is a trivial generating set. A more interesting case is when the generating set is much smaller than the group itself.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    It can be verified that 𝐷6 =⟨𝑠,𝑟⟩D6=⟨s,r⟩, that is, any symmetric operation of an equilateral triangle can be obtained through composition of rotations and reflections.

    Cyclic Groups

    The structure of groups generated by a single element is very simple. Such groups are called cyclic groups.

    Cyclic Group

    For a group 𝐺G, if there exists 𝑥 ∈𝐺x∈G such that 𝐺 =⟨𝑥⟩G=⟨x⟩, then 𝐺G is called a cyclic group.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    All non-trivial subgroups of 𝐷6D6 and {𝑒}{e} are cyclic groups.

    It can be proven that the structure of cyclic groups is uniquely determined by their size. If a cyclic group is infinite, then it must have the same group structure as the additive group of integers (𝐙, +)(Z,+), denoted 𝐶∞C∞ or 𝐙Z; otherwise, let the number of elements in the group be 𝑛 ∈𝐍+n∈N+, then it must have the same group structure as the additive group of congruence classes of integers modulo 𝑛n (𝐙/𝑛𝐙, +)(Z/nZ,+), denoted 𝐶𝑛Cn or 𝐙𝑛Zn. The strict statement of this conclusion requires the concept of group isomorphism below, which strictly describes when two group structures are the same.

    Classification Theorem for Cyclic Groups

    A finite cyclic group 𝐺G of size 𝑛n is isomorphic to 𝐶𝑛Cn; an infinite cyclic group 𝐺G is isomorphic to 𝐶∞C∞.

    Proof

    Given a cyclic group 𝐺 =⟨𝑥⟩G=⟨x⟩, it can always be written as 𝐺 ={𝑥𝑛 :𝑛 ∈𝐙}G={xn:n∈Z}. If 𝐺G is finite, then there exist natural numbers 𝑛 <𝑚n<m such that 𝑥𝑛 =𝑥𝑚xn=xm. By the cancellation law, we can get 𝑥𝑚−𝑛 =𝑒xm−n=e. At this time, let the smallest positive integer 𝑛 ∈𝐍+n∈N+ such that 𝑥𝑛 =𝑒xn=e, then the sequence {𝑥𝑘}{xk} will cycle with length 𝑛n, and elements within a cycle are all different (otherwise it would violate the minimality of 𝑛n). At this time, the map 𝑥𝑘 ↦¯𝑘xk↦k¯ provides the isomorphism 𝐺 →𝐙/𝑛𝐙G→Z/nZ, i.e., 𝐺 ≅𝐶𝑛G≅Cn. Conversely, if 𝐺G is infinite, then elements in 𝐺G are all different, and the map 𝑥𝑘 ↦𝑘xk↦k provides the isomorphism 𝐺 →𝐙G→Z, i.e., 𝐺 ≅𝐶∞G≅C∞.

    All cyclic groups are abelian groups. The example 𝐷6D6 in this article shows that even if all non-trivial subgroups of a group are cyclic, the group itself may not be abelian.

    Order

    The order of a group is the number of elements in the group. The order of a given element in the group is the order of the cyclic subgroup generated by that element. From this, we have the following definitions:

    Order of a Group

    The order of a group 𝐺G is the number of its elements, denoted |𝐺||G|. The order of an infinite group is also infinite.

    Order of an Element

    The order of an element 𝑥 ∈𝐺x∈G in group 𝐺G is the smallest positive integer 𝑛n such that 𝑥𝑛 =𝑒xn=e holds, denoted |𝑥||x|; if such 𝑛n does not exist, then the order of 𝑥x is infinite, denoted |𝑥| =∞|x|=∞.

    The order of an element is always not greater than the order of the group. In fact, as proved below, the order of an element always divides the order of the group. However, the order of the group is not always the maximum order of elements in the group. For example, 𝐷6D6 is a group of order 6, but the maximum order of elements is 3. The order of the group is also not the least common multiple of the orders of all elements. For example, the order of the Klein four-group[^klein] 𝑉4V4 is 4, but it only has elements of order 1 and order 2.

    Theorem

    In a finite cyclic group 𝐶𝑛 =⟨𝑥⟩Cn=⟨x⟩, the order of the element 𝑥𝑘xk is

    𝑛gcd(𝑘,𝑛).ngcd(k,n).

    In particular, the number of generators of 𝐶𝑛Cn is 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n), where 𝜑( ⋅)φ(⋅) is the Euler totient function.

    As an application of the discussion above, note that the order of the multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑛n is 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n), and any element 𝑎a in the group has an order dividing it. Therefore, there must be 𝑎𝜑(𝑛) =1aφ(n)=1. This is Euler's theorem, because elements in this group are precisely all elements coprime with 𝑛n.

    Cosets

    Elements outside subgroups also have structure in the group.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    Observe the subgroup ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩ in 𝐷6D6, the remaining elements {𝑠,𝑠𝑟,𝑠𝑟2}{s,sr,sr2} have a structure very similar to ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩: each operation in it can be obtained by composing 𝑠s with operations in ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩. Similarly, considering the subgroup ⟨𝑠⟩⟨s⟩, the remaining elements in the group can be divided into two categories, {𝑟,𝑠𝑟}{r,sr} and {𝑟2,𝑠𝑟2}{r2,sr2}, which can be obtained by composing elements in ⟨𝑠⟩⟨s⟩ with 𝑟r and 𝑟2r2 respectively. This phenomenon is universal.

    Given a subgroup, we can define its cosets.

    Coset

    Let 𝐺G be a group and 𝐻 ≤𝐺H≤G be its subgroup. The left coset and right coset of the subgroup 𝐻H containing 𝑔g are respectively defined as the sets

    𝑔𝐻={𝑔ℎ:ℎ∈𝐻},𝐻𝑔={ℎ𝑔:ℎ∈𝐻}.gH={gh:h∈H},Hg={hg:h∈H}.

    Elements in a coset are called representatives of the coset.

    The subgroup itself is also its coset. Given a subgroup, all cosets form a partition of the group, i.e., the group is a disjoint union of all cosets. A partition can always be viewed as equivalence classes of some equivalence relation. For the partition of left cosets, this equivalence relation is 𝑔1 ∼𝑔2g1∼g2 if and only if 𝑔−11𝑔2 ∈𝐻g1−1g2∈H; for the partition of right cosets, this equivalence relation is 𝑔1 ∼𝑔2g1∼g2 if and only if 𝑔1𝑔−12 ∈𝐻g1g2−1∈H.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    In the language of cosets, in the example above, 𝐷6D6 can be divided into ⟨𝑟⟩ ∪𝑠⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩∪s⟨r⟩ and ⟨𝑠⟩ ∪⟨𝑠⟩𝑟 ∪⟨𝑠⟩𝑟2⟨s⟩∪⟨s⟩r∪⟨s⟩r2. The former divides the group into several left cosets, and the latter into several right cosets. It should be noted that the choice of representatives is not special. For example, it can be verified that 𝑠⟨𝑟⟩ =𝑠𝑟⟨𝑟\ranglelefts⟨r⟩=sr⟨r\rangleleft. Any element in a coset is a representative of that coset.

    Different cosets of the same subgroup all have the same size, equal to the size of the corresponding subgroup. Since all cosets of a given subgroup form a partition of the group, the order of a finite group must be an integer multiple of the order of the subgroup. This is called Lagrange's theorem.

    Lagrange's Theorem

    For a finite group 𝐺G and its subgroup 𝐻 ≤𝐺H≤G, we have |𝐺| =[𝐺 :𝐻]|𝐻||G|=[G:H]|H|, where [𝐺 :𝐻][G:H] denotes the number of left (right) cosets of subgroup 𝐻H in group 𝐺G, called the index of subgroup 𝐻H in 𝐺G.

    Proof

    Consider the map ℎ ↦𝑔ℎh↦gh of left multiplication by 𝑔g. It and the map ℎ ↦𝑔−1ℎh↦g−1h are inverses of each other, so they are both bijections. This shows that |𝐻| =|𝑔𝐻||H|=|gH| always holds.

    Note that the order of an element is the order of the cyclic subgroup generated by that element, so the order of an element also necessarily divides the order of the group.

    Normal Subgroups

    In general, the left and right cosets of a given subgroup are not the same.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    In group 𝐷6D6, ⟨𝑠⟩𝑟 ={𝑟,𝑠𝑟}⟨s⟩r={r,sr}, but 𝑟⟨𝑠⟩ ={𝑟,𝑠𝑟2}r⟨s⟩={r,sr2}. However, if we consider the subgroup ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩, then left and right cosets are always the same, because at this time the group has only two cosets, and as a coset, the subgroup necessarily coincides.

    Whether left and right cosets are the same reflects the properties of the corresponding subgroup.

    Normal Subgroup

    Let 𝑁 ≤𝐺N≤G be a subgroup of group 𝐺G. If for all ℎ ∈𝑁h∈N and 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G, we have 𝑔ℎ𝑔−1 ∈𝑁ghg−1∈N, in other words, for all 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G, we have 𝑔𝑁𝑔−1 ⊆𝑁gNg−1⊆N, then 𝑁N is called a normal subgroup of 𝐺G, denoted 𝑁 ⊴𝐺N⊴G.

    The condition in this definition is exactly equivalent to 𝑔𝑁 =𝑁𝑔gN=Ng always holding. Group 𝐺G always has trivial normal subgroups, namely ⟨𝑒⟩⟨e⟩ and 𝐺G itself.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    In group 𝐷6D6, ⟨𝑠⟩⟨s⟩ is not a normal subgroup, while ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩ is a normal subgroup.

    Quotient Groups

    Normal subgroups are a very important type of subgroups, one reason being that quotient groups can be defined based on normal subgroups.

    For a group 𝐺G and its normal subgroup 𝑁 ⊴𝐺N⊴G, consider the set of all cosets

    𝐺/𝑁={𝑔𝑁:𝑔∈𝐺}.G/N={gN:g∈G}.

    At this time, left and right cosets are the same, so we do not need to distinguish them. Starting from the operation of group 𝐺G, we can define a binary operation ∘∘ on 𝐺/𝑁G/N, which satisfies

    𝑔1𝑁∘𝑔2𝑁=(𝑔1𝑔2)𝑁.g1N∘g2N=(g1g2)N.

    It can be proven that the result of the operation is independent of the choice of representatives[^quotient]. At this time, (𝐺/𝑁, ∘)(G/N,∘) indeed has the structure of a group, which is called the quotient group (or factor group) of 𝐺G modulo 𝑁N. The quotient group 𝐺/𝑁G/N is not a subgroup of group 𝐺G; each element of it is a subset of group 𝐺G.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    In group 𝐷6D6, the meaning of the quotient group 𝐺/⟨𝑟⟩G/⟨r⟩ is very obvious. It is equivalent to, among all these symmetric operations, ignoring the angle by which the triangle is rotated, and only caring about whether it flips the triangle. The composition of two operations that both flip the triangle is equivalent to not flipping the original triangle; however, if one operation flips the triangle and the other does not, then the composition necessarily flips the triangle. Whether to flip also has group structure. Ignoring the details of rotation in group 𝐷6D6 and only considering the presence or absence of flipping is, algebraically, modding out ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩ from the complex group 𝐷6D6 to get the quotient group 𝐷6/⟨𝑟⟩D6/⟨r⟩. These statements do not hold for the subgroup ⟨𝑠⟩⟨s⟩, because if we ignore whether flipping happens, the degree of rotation cannot be definitively determined, which is also why 𝐺/⟨𝑠⟩G/⟨s⟩ does not have quotient group structure.

    Quotient groups can simplify complex groups, allowing observation of part of the group's structure to understand the original group's structure. This is also why quotient groups are also called factor groups. Groups that contain no other normal subgroups besides trivial normal subgroups are called simple groups. These groups cannot be simplified into smaller groups. Like prime numbers, they are the building blocks for forming more complex group structures.

    Group Homomorphisms

    The second method to understand the structure of a given group is to compare the structures of two groups.

    For two groups, to compare their structures is to construct a mapping between the two groups. However, such a mapping cannot be arbitrary; it must preserve the structure of the group, i.e., the operation of the group must be consistent before and after the mapping. Such a mapping is called a group homomorphism.

    Group Homomorphism

    Let the map 𝜑 :𝐺 →𝐻φ:G→H be a mapping from group (𝐺, ⋅)(G,⋅) to group (𝐻, ⊙)(H,⊙). If 𝜑φ preserves the group operation, i.e., for all 𝑔1,𝑔2 ∈𝐺g1,g2∈G, 𝜑(𝑔1 ⋅𝑔2) =𝜑(𝑔1) ⊙𝜑(𝑔2)φ(g1⋅g2)=φ(g1)⊙φ(g2), then the map 𝜑φ is called a homomorphism from group 𝐺G to group 𝐻H.

    Group homomorphisms necessarily map the identity element to the identity element, and also necessarily map inverse elements to inverse elements.

    Notation

    Below, if there is no ambiguity, we will not distinguish the operation notation in groups 𝐺G and 𝐻H, and for simplicity, we will omit these notations.

    Group Isomorphisms

    For a homomorphism 𝜑 :𝐺 →𝐻φ:G→H from group 𝐺G to group 𝐻H, a natural question is the extent to which this homomorphism reflects that the structures of group 𝐺G and group 𝐻H are the same. For this, we examine the image 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) of group 𝐺G under the homomorphism 𝜑φ. On one hand, 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) is a subgroup of group 𝐻H; but if 𝜑φ is not surjective, 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) is not the same as group 𝐻H. On the other hand, 𝜑φ is also not necessarily injective; if 𝜑φ is not injective, then 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) only reflects part of the structure of group 𝐺G. Only when 𝜑φ is a bijection are the structures of group 𝐺G and group 𝐻H completely the same. This special type of group homomorphism is called a group isomorphism.

    Group Isomorphism

    Let 𝜑 :𝐺 →𝐻φ:G→H be a homomorphism from group 𝐺G to group 𝐻H. If 𝜑φ is a bijection, then 𝜑φ is called an isomorphism between group 𝐺G and group 𝐻H, denoted 𝐺 ≅𝐻G≅H.

    The structures of two isomorphic groups are completely the same. If we only care about the structure of groups, there is no need to distinguish two isomorphic groups. The classification theorem for cyclic groups given earlier is stated in the sense of isomorphism.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    Returning to the earlier example, each symmetric operation of an equilateral triangle uniquely corresponds to a permutation operation on the set of vertices. All permutations on the vertex set also form a group, i.e., 𝑆3S3. It is easy to verify that the mapping 𝜑 :𝐷6 →𝑆3φ:D6→S3 obtained is a group homomorphism; furthermore, it is also a group isomorphism. So, 𝐷6 ≅𝑆3D6≅S3. In fact, groups of order 6 are either isomorphic to 𝐶6C6 or isomorphic to 𝑆3S3 (proof below).

    Classifying the structures of finite groups of a given order is an important research topic in group theory but is beyond the scope of this article.

    Kernel of a Homomorphism

    For a general homomorphism, we can further discuss how much information about the group's structure is lost in the homomorphism. Continuing with the notation above. We know 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) is a subgroup of group 𝐻H. Now the key question is the relationship between 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) and group 𝐺G.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    Consider the mapping 𝜑 :𝐷6 →𝐶2 =⟨𝑥⟩φ:D6→C2=⟨x⟩ defined as follows:

    𝜑(𝑒)=𝜑(𝑟)=𝜑(𝑟2)=𝑒, 𝜑(𝑠)=𝜑(𝑠𝑟)=𝜑(𝑠𝑟2)=𝑥.φ(e)=φ(r)=φ(r2)=e, φ(s)=φ(sr)=φ(sr2)=x.

    It is easy to verify that 𝜑φ is a group homomorphism; it is surjective but not injective. Its meaning is very obvious: it maps each symmetric operation of the group to whether it flips. The information compressed in this homomorphism about group 𝐷6D6 is the information about its rotation angle. For example, if there is no flip, rotation at any angle maps to the identity element in group 𝐶2C2.

    This example inspires using the preimage of {𝑒}{e} to measure the structural information lost in the homomorphism. From this, we have the following definition.

    Kernel of a Homomorphism

    Let 𝜑 :𝐺 →𝐻φ:G→H be a homomorphism from group 𝐺G to group 𝐻H. The kernel of the homomorphism 𝜑φ is ker⁡𝜑 ={𝑔 ∈𝐺 :𝜑(𝑔) =𝑒}ker⁡φ={g∈G:φ(g)=e}, where 𝑒e is the identity element of 𝐻H.

    Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms

    The kernel ker⁡𝜑ker⁡φ indeed characterizes the structural information lost in the group homomorphism. The precise statement of this conclusion is the Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms (also called First Isomorphism Theorem).

    Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms (First Isomorphism Theorem)

    Let 𝜑 :𝐺 →𝐻φ:G→H be a homomorphism from group 𝐺G to group 𝐻H. Then ker⁡𝜑 ⊴𝐺ker⁡φ⊴G, and 𝐺/ker⁡𝜑 ≅𝜑(𝐺) ≤𝐻G/ker⁡φ≅φ(G)≤H.

    Proof

    First, 𝑁 =ker⁡𝜑N=ker⁡φ is a normal subgroup, because for any ℎ ∈𝑁h∈N, we have 𝜑(𝑔ℎ𝑔−1) =𝜑(𝑔)𝜑(ℎ)𝜑(𝑔)−1 =𝜑(𝑔)𝜑(𝑔)−1 =𝑒φ(ghg−1)=φ(g)φ(h)φ(g)−1=φ(g)φ(g)−1=e, i.e., 𝑔ℎ𝑔−1 ∈ker⁡𝜑ghg−1∈ker⁡φ. Then, consider the mapping Φ :𝐺/𝑁 →𝜑(𝐺)Φ:G/N→φ(G) satisfying Φ(𝑔𝑁) =𝜑(𝑔)Φ(gN)=φ(g). The mapping is well-defined because if 𝑔1𝑁 =𝑔2𝑁g1N=g2N, then 𝑔−11𝑔2 ∈𝑁g1−1g2∈N, so 𝜑(𝑔−11𝑔2) =𝑒φ(g1−1g2)=e, i.e., 𝜑(𝑔1) =𝜑(𝑔2)φ(g1)=φ(g2). ΦΦ is clearly surjective; it is also injective because ker⁡Φ ={𝑔𝑁 :𝜑(𝑔) =𝑒} ={𝑁}ker⁡Φ={gN:φ(g)=e}={N}. Therefore, ΦΦ is a group isomorphism. Finally, 𝜑(𝑔1)𝜑(𝑔2)−1 =𝜑(𝑔1𝑔−12) ∈𝜑(𝐺)φ(g1)φ(g2)−1=φ(g1g2−1)∈φ(G), and by the subgroup criterion, 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) must be a subgroup.

    Corollary

    The homomorphism 𝜑 :𝐺 →𝐻φ:G→H is injective if and only if ker⁡𝜑 ={𝑒}ker⁡φ={e}. At this time, 𝐺G is isomorphic to a subgroup of 𝐻H, i.e., 𝐺 ≅𝜑(𝐺) ≤𝐻G≅φ(G)≤H.

    That is, the kernel of a homomorphism 𝜑φ is a normal subgroup of group 𝐺G, and the quotient group 𝐺/ker⁡𝜑G/ker⁡φ obtained by modding out ker⁡𝜑ker⁡φ is isomorphic to the image of the homomorphism 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G), and this image is precisely a subgroup of group 𝐻H.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    The kernel of the group homomorphism 𝜑 :𝐷6 →𝐶2φ:D6→C2 given above is ⟨𝑟⟩⟨r⟩, and in the earlier discussion of normal subgroups, it has already been shown that 𝐷6/⟨𝑟⟩D6/⟨r⟩ is indeed isomorphic to 𝐶2C2.

    Natural Homomorphisms

    This conclusion is not surprising. This is because in constructing the homomorphism 𝜑 :𝐷6 →𝐶2φ:D6→C2, we used precisely the geometric meaning of the quotient group 𝐷6/⟨𝑟⟩D6/⟨r⟩. This phenomenon is not rare. In fact, for every quotient group, we can construct a group homomorphism such that the image of this homomorphism is isomorphic to the given quotient group.

    Natural Homomorphism

    For a group 𝐺G and its normal subgroup 𝑁 ⊴𝐺N⊴G, the mapping 𝜋 :𝐺 →𝐺/𝑁π:G→G/N given by 𝜋(𝑔) =𝑔𝑁π(g)=gN is a surjective homomorphism from 𝐺G to 𝐺/𝑁G/N, called the natural homomorphism or natural map from 𝐺G to the quotient group 𝐺/𝑁G/N.

    This conclusion also shows that for any given normal subgroup of a group, we can find a corresponding group homomorphism such that the kernel of this homomorphism is exactly the given normal subgroup. The Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms shows that any kernel is a normal subgroup. Therefore, normal subgroups and kernels of homomorphisms are two sides of the same coin.

    Using the concept of natural maps, the Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms actually says that the following commutative diagram holds.

    Here, all arrows are group homomorphisms, and 𝑁 =ker⁡𝜑N=ker⁡φ is the kernel of homomorphism 𝜑φ, 𝜑(𝐺)φ(G) is the image of homomorphism 𝜑φ. These mappings in order are: 𝜋 :𝑔 ↦𝑔𝑁π:g↦gN is the natural map from group 𝐺G to the quotient group 𝐺/𝑁G/N (surjective homomorphism), Φ :𝑔𝑁 ↦𝜑(𝑔)Φ:gN↦φ(g) is the isomorphism mapping, and 𝜄ι is the embedding map (injective homomorphism). The commutative diagram means that the result of composing the mappings along two different paths from 𝐺G to 𝐻H is consistent, i.e., 𝜑 =𝜄 ∘Φ ∘𝜋φ=ι∘Φ∘π. The commutative diagram clearly shows that the information lost in 𝜑φ is reflected in 𝜋π and 𝜄ι.

    Isomorphism Theorems of Groups

    Powerful tools for understanding the structure of groups are the isomorphism theorems of groups. The first isomorphism theorem has been given above. To complete the content, here are other common isomorphism theorems.

    The second isomorphism theorem involves the concept of the product of subsets.

    Product of Subsets

    For a group 𝐺G and its subsets 𝐴,𝐵 ⊆𝐺A,B⊆G, the product of subsets 𝐴A and 𝐵B is the subset 𝐴𝐵 ={𝑎𝑏 :𝑎 ∈𝐴,𝑏 ∈𝐵}AB={ab:a∈A,b∈B}.

    The product of subgroups is not always a subgroup. For example, in group 𝐷6D6, the product of subgroup 𝐴 =⟨𝑠⟩A=⟨s⟩ and subgroup 𝐵 =⟨𝑠𝑟⟩B=⟨sr⟩ equals 𝐴𝐵 ={𝑒,𝑠,𝑟,𝑠𝑟}AB={e,s,r,sr}, which is not a subgroup of 𝐺G because (𝑠𝑟)𝑠 =𝑟2 ∉𝐴𝐵(sr)s=r2∉AB. In fact, such counterexamples where 𝑎 ∈𝐴a∈A, 𝑏 ∈𝐵b∈B, but 𝑏𝑎 ∉𝐴𝐵ba∉AB are the fundamental reason why the product is not a subgroup. For this, we have the following theorem.

    Theorem

    For a group 𝐺G and its subgroups 𝐴,𝐵 ≤𝐺A,B≤G, the product 𝐴𝐵AB is a subgroup if and only if 𝐴𝐵 =𝐵𝐴AB=BA.

    Proof

    If 𝐴𝐵AB is a subgroup, then we necessarily have 𝑏𝑎 =(𝑎−1𝑏−1)−1 ∈𝐴𝐵ba=(a−1b−1)−1∈AB for any 𝑎 ∈𝐴a∈A and 𝑏 ∈𝐵b∈B, so 𝐵𝐴 ⊆𝐴𝐵BA⊆AB. Conversely, if 𝐴𝐵 =𝐵𝐴AB=BA, then for any 𝑎1,𝑎2 ∈𝐴a1,a2∈A and 𝑏1,𝑏2 ∈𝐵b1,b2∈B, we have (𝑎1𝑏1)(𝑎2𝑏2)−1 =𝑎1𝑏1𝑏−12𝑎−12 ∈𝑎1𝐵𝐴 =𝑎1𝐴𝐵 =𝐴𝐵(a1b1)(a2b2)−1=a1b1b2−1a2−1∈a1BA=a1AB=AB, so by the subgroup criterion, 𝐴𝐵AB is necessarily a subgroup.

    The Second Isomorphism Theorem (also called the diamond isomorphism theorem) gives a simpler sufficient condition for the product of subgroups to still be a subgroup, and further determines its structure.

    Second Isomorphism Theorem

    Let group 𝐺G have subgroups 𝐴,𝐵 ≤𝐺A,B≤G satisfying 𝐴 ≤𝑁𝐺(𝐵)A≤NG(B). Then 𝐴𝐵 ≤𝐺AB≤G, and 𝐵 ⊴𝐴𝐵B⊴AB, 𝐴 ∩𝐵 ⊴𝐴A∩B⊴A, 𝐴𝐵/𝐵 ≅𝐴/(𝐴 ∩𝐵)AB/B≅A/(A∩B). Here, 𝑁𝐺(𝐵)NG(B) is the normalizer of 𝐵B. A sufficient condition for 𝐴 ≤𝑁𝐺(𝐵)A≤NG(B) is 𝐵 ⊴𝐺B⊴G.

    Proof

    Since 𝐴 ≤𝑁𝐺(𝐵)A≤NG(B), necessarily 𝑎𝐵𝑎−1 =𝐵aBa−1=B holds for all 𝑎 ∈𝐴a∈A, i.e., 𝑎𝐵 =𝐵𝑎aB=Ba. Therefore, necessarily 𝐴𝐵 =𝐵𝐴AB=BA, so by the above theorem, 𝐴𝐵AB is a subgroup. As a subgroup of 𝐴𝐵AB, 𝐵B has the same left and right cosets, so 𝐵 ⊴𝐴𝐵B⊴AB.

    Consider the mapping 𝜑 :𝐴 →𝐴𝐵/𝐵φ:A→AB/B satisfying 𝜑(𝑎) =𝑎𝐵φ(a)=aB. This is a surjection, and its kernel ker⁡𝜑 ={𝑎 ∈𝐴 :𝑎𝐵 =𝐵} =𝐴 ∩𝐵ker⁡φ={a∈A:aB=B}=A∩B. Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms gives the result.

    The Third Isomorphism Theorem gives the correspondence between normal subgroups of quotient groups and those of original groups. It explains the reasonableness of the idea of further decomposing quotient groups.

    Third Isomorphism Theorem

    Let group 𝐺G have normal subgroups 𝐻,𝐾 ⊴𝐺H,K⊴G, and 𝐻 ≤𝐾H≤K. Then 𝐾/𝐻 ⊴𝐺/𝐻K/H⊴G/H, and (𝐺/𝐻)/(𝐾/𝐻) ≅𝐺/𝐾(G/H)/(K/H)≅G/K.

    Proof

    Consider the mapping 𝜑 :𝐺/𝐻 →𝐺/𝐾φ:G/H→G/K satisfying 𝜑(𝑔𝐻) =𝑔𝐾φ(gH)=gK. This is a surjective group homomorphism, and ker⁡𝜑 ={𝑔𝐻 :𝑔 ∈𝐾} =𝐾/𝐻ker⁡φ={gH:g∈K}=K/H. Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms gives the result.

    This conclusion can be extended to the Fourth Isomorphism Theorem, also called the Correspondence Theorem. It further gives the correspondence between the subgroup lattice of the group and the subgroup lattice of the quotient group.

    Correspondence Theorem

    Let group 𝐺G have normal subgroup 𝑁 ⊴𝐺N⊴G. Then there is a bijection 𝜑 :H →Sφ:H→S between the set of all subgroups H ={𝐻 :𝑁 ⊆𝐻 ⊆𝐺}H={H:N⊆H⊆G} of 𝐺G containing 𝑁N and the set of all subgroups S ={𝑆 :𝑆 ≤𝐺/𝑁}S={S:S≤G/N} of 𝐺/𝑁G/N. This bijection maps 𝐻 ∈HH∈H to 𝐻/𝑁 ∈SH/N∈S. This bijection preserves subgroup inclusion, and normal subgroups of 𝐺G always map to normal subgroups of 𝐺/𝑁G/N.

    On the Content and Names of Isomorphism Theorems

    Different textbooks may have different content and names for group isomorphism theorems. The version taken here is a common one. Wikipedia summarizes the differences in content and names of isomorphism theorems in common textbooks.

    Group Actions

    The third method to understand the structure of a given group is to examine the action of the group on a set.

    For example, the spatial symmetry group of an equilateral triangle discussed in this article is defined through the action of group elements (i.e., symmetric operations) on the triangle. Likewise, the definition of the symmetric group 𝑆𝑀SM can be given through the action of its elements on the set 𝑀M. Here, the action refers to each element of the group corresponding to a permutation on the set.

    Group Action on a Set

    For a group 𝐺G, a set 𝑋X, and a mapping 𝐺 ×𝑋 →𝑋G×X→X, where the image of (𝑔,𝑥)(g,x) under this mapping is denoted 𝑔 ⋅𝑥g⋅x. If this mapping satisfies 𝑔1 ⋅(𝑔2 ⋅𝑥) =(𝑔1𝑔2) ⋅𝑥g1⋅(g2⋅x)=(g1g2)⋅x and 𝑒 ⋅𝑥 =𝑥e⋅x=x for all 𝑔1,𝑔2 ∈𝐺g1,g2∈G and 𝑥 ∈𝑋x∈X, then this mapping is called a group action of group 𝐺G on set 𝑋X.

    "Left Action" and "Right Action"

    The definition of group action taken here is called left action in some sources[^group-action], because in the notation 𝑔 ⋅𝑥g⋅x, the group element is written on the left side of the set element. Correspondingly, when the group element 𝑔1𝑔2g1g2 acts on the set, we need to perform 𝑔2g2's action first, then 𝑔1g1's action. Of course, right action can be correspondingly defined and denoted 𝑥 ⋅𝑔x⋅g. At this time, the order of group element composition in left action is opposite, i.e., 𝑥 ⋅(𝑔1𝑔2) =(𝑥 ⋅𝑔1) ⋅𝑔2x⋅(g1g2)=(x⋅g1)⋅g2. The two differ only in notation, not in essence. Therefore, this article defaults to the left action notation.

    For group actions satisfying the above definition, we naturally have the following construction

    𝜑:𝐺→𝑆𝑋𝑔↦𝜑𝑔:𝑋→𝑋𝑥↦𝑔⋅𝑥.φ:G→SXg↦φg:X→Xx↦g⋅x.

    This mapping maps each element 𝑔g in group 𝐺G to a permutation 𝜑𝑔φg on set 𝑋X, and permutation 𝜑𝑔φg maps element 𝑥x to 𝑔 ⋅𝑥g⋅x.

    According to the definition, the identity element 𝑒e in the group corresponds to the bijection 𝜑𝑒φe which is the identity mapping on 𝑋X, and the mapping 𝜑𝑔φg corresponding to a group element 𝑔g and the mapping 𝜑𝑔−1φg−1 corresponding to its inverse element 𝑔−1g−1 are inverses of each other (this also explains why 𝜑𝑔φg is always a bijection). It can be verified that 𝜑𝑔1𝑔2 =𝜑𝑔1𝜑𝑔2φg1g2=φg1φg2, i.e., 𝜑φ is a group homomorphism from group 𝐺G to group 𝑆𝑋SX.

    This group homomorphism 𝜑φ is called the permutation representation of the group action. It maps group 𝐺G to some permutation group.

    Permutation Group

    If group 𝐺G is a subgroup of some symmetric group, then group 𝐺G is called a permutation group.

    The kernel of this group homomorphism is also called the kernel of the group action. If this group homomorphism has a trivial kernel, i.e., this homomorphism is injective, then the group action is called faithful, i.e., the permutation representation faithfully reflects the group's structural information. At this time, group 𝐺G is isomorphic to the permutation group obtained from the permutation representation.

    Notation

    Below, for the sake of simplicity, we will omit the ⋅⋅ notation in group actions.

    Orbits

    Group actions are binary mappings. Fixing an element 𝑔g in the group, we can obtain a permutation on the set. And if we fix an element 𝑥x on the set, we can obtain all possible results of the group acting on that element.

    Orbit

    For a group action of 𝐺G on set 𝑋X and 𝑥 ∈𝑋x∈X, the orbit of 𝑥x under the action of group 𝐺G is the subset 𝐺𝑥 ={𝑔𝑥 :𝑔 ∈𝐺}Gx={gx:g∈G}.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    For example, if we consider the action of subgroup ⟨𝑠⟩ ≤𝐷6⟨s⟩≤D6 on the set of vertices of an equilateral triangle, then the orbit of vertex 11 is {1}{1}, and vertices 22 and 33 have the orbit {2,3}{2,3}. However, the action of subgroup ⟨𝑟⟩ ≤𝐷6⟨r⟩≤D6 on the set of vertices has only one orbit, i.e., the entire set of vertices.

    It is easy to prove that under the action of group 𝐺G, all orbits of set 𝑋X form a partition of that set, denoted 𝑋/𝐺X/G. However, different from cosets, these orbits are not necessarily of equal length.

    Stabilizers

    Under group action, the length of the orbit of an element in the set depends on how many elements in the group correspond to permutations that fix it.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    For example, why is it that under the action of subgroup ⟨𝑠⟩ ≤𝐷6⟨s⟩≤D6, the orbit of vertex 11 has length 1? Because all elements in the group map vertex 11 to itself. And the orbit of vertex 22 has length 2, because only the identity element 𝑒e maps vertex 22 to itself.

    This inspires the following definition.

    Stabilizer

    For a group action of 𝐺G on set 𝑋X and 𝑥 ∈𝑋x∈X, the stabilizer of 𝑥x in group 𝐺G is the subgroup 𝐺𝑥 ={𝑔 ∈𝐺 :𝑔𝑥 =𝑥}Gx={g∈G:gx=x}.

    The kernel of a group action is the intersection of the stabilizers of all elements in the set.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    Consider the group action of 𝐷6D6 on the set of vertices. Then the stabilizer of vertex 11 is {𝑒,𝑠} =⟨𝑠⟩{e,s}=⟨s⟩. This is a subgroup of 𝐷6D6. Since 𝐷6D6 can be divided into left cosets ⟨𝑠⟩⟨s⟩, 𝑟⟨𝑠⟩r⟨s⟩, and 𝑟2⟨𝑠⟩r2⟨s⟩, it is easy to find that each left coset has the same result when acting on vertex 11.

    This example shows that elements on the orbit correspond one-to-one with left cosets of the stabilizer. This shows the following result.

    Theorem

    For a group action of 𝐺G on set 𝑋X, for element 𝑥 ∈𝑋x∈X, the stabilizer 𝐺𝑥Gx is a subgroup of 𝐺G, and there is a bijection between left cosets of subgroup 𝐺𝑥Gx and the orbit 𝐺𝑥Gx.

    Proof

    Verify that the mapping 𝑔𝐺𝑥 ↦𝑔𝑥gGx↦gx is a well-defined bijection.

    Using Lagrange's theorem, we can connect the length of the orbit with the number of cosets of the stabilizer. This is the Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem.

    Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem

    For a finite group 𝐺G acting on set 𝑋X and 𝑥 ∈𝑋x∈X, we have |𝐺𝑥| =[𝐺 :𝐺𝑥] =|𝐺|/|𝐺𝑥||Gx|=[G:Gx]=|G|/|Gx|.

    This conclusion can be verified in the example above.

    Burnside's Lemma

    This lemma gives the formula for the number of orbits of a group action.

    Burnside's Lemma

    For a group action of 𝐺G on set 𝑋X, the number of orbits equals the average number of fixed points of elements in the group, i.e.,

    |𝑋/𝐺|=1|𝐺|∑𝑔∈𝐺|𝑋𝑔|.|X/G|=1|G|∑g∈G|Xg|.

    Here, 𝑋𝑔 ={𝑥 ∈𝑋 :𝑔𝑥 =𝑥}Xg={x∈X:gx=x} is the set of fixed points of the permutation corresponding to 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G.

    Proof

    The proof of this theorem is quite concise. Note that the number of orbits can be written as

    |𝑋/𝐺|=∑𝑜∈𝑋/𝐺1=∑𝑥∈𝑋1|𝐺𝑥|=1|𝐺|∑𝑥∈𝑋|𝐺𝑥|.|X/G|=∑o∈X/G1=∑x∈X1|Gx|=1|G|∑x∈X|Gx|.

    The last equality is the corollary above; the right-hand side differs from what we need to prove only by the Fubini theorem because the summation in both is a count of the set {(𝑔,𝑥) ∈𝐺 ×𝑋 :𝑔𝑥 =𝑥}{(g,x)∈G×X:gx=x}, except that on the right we sum over 𝑔g first, while on the left we sum over 𝑥x first.

    This theorem has many applications in combinatorics and can be used to count the number of "essentially different" objects. More examples and discussions can be found in Pólya Counting.

    Cayley's Theorem

    To study the structure of groups using group actions, we need to choose appropriate sets. In fact, the group itself is such a set. Therefore, next we consider two common types of group actions of a group on itself, and use them to analyze the structure of the group.

    The first such group action is left multiplication of the group on itself. Its permutation representation is as follows.

    𝜑:𝐺→𝑆𝐺𝑔↦𝜑𝑔:𝐺→𝐺𝑥↦𝑔𝑥φ:G→SGg↦φg:G→Gx↦gx

    The left multiplication action of a group is necessarily faithful because groups satisfy the cancellation law. Therefore, by the Fundamental Theorem of Homomorphisms, 𝐺G can be embedded into the symmetric group 𝑆𝐺SG. This shows that every group is isomorphic to some permutation group[^cayley].

    Cayley's Theorem

    Group 𝐺G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group 𝑆𝐺SG.

    This group action has only one orbit, and the stabilizer of each element is {𝑒}{e}.

    Conjugation

    The second action of a group on itself is called conjugation. Its permutation representation is as follows.

    𝜑:𝐺→𝑆𝐺𝑔↦𝜑𝑔:𝐺→𝐺𝑥↦𝑔𝑥𝑔−1φ:G→SGg↦φg:G→Gx↦gxg−1

    Under conjugation in the group, orbits and stabilizers both have special names.

    Conjugacy Class

    For group 𝐺G and 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G, the conjugacy class of element 𝑔g in group 𝐺G is the orbit of 𝑔g under conjugation. If elements 𝑔g and ℎh are in the same conjugacy class, then 𝑔g and ℎh are called conjugates.

    Centralizer

    For group 𝐺G and 𝑎 ∈𝐺a∈G, the centralizer of element 𝑎a in group 𝐺G is 𝐶𝐺(𝑎) ={𝑔 ∈𝐺 :𝑔𝑎 =𝑎𝑔}CG(a)={g∈G:ga=ag}.

    Center

    For a group 𝐺G, the center of group 𝑎a is 𝑍(𝐺) = ∩𝑎∈𝐺𝐶𝐺(𝑎) ={𝑔 ∈𝐺 :∀𝑎 ∈𝐺(𝑔𝑎 =𝑎𝑔)}Z(G)=∩a∈GCG(a)={g∈G:∀a∈G(ga=ag)}.

    The center of a group is the set of elements that commute with all elements in the group; because it is the kernel of the group action, it is necessarily a normal subgroup. The size of the center of a group indicates how far it is from being an abelian group. The centralizer of a given element is the set of all elements that commute with that element; it is also the largest among all subgroups containing it, which is also the origin of its name. Meanwhile, because it is the stabilizer of an element under conjugation, it is a subgroup. Conjugacy classes are generally not subgroups.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    Returning to group 𝐷6D6, its center is {𝑒} ≠𝐺{e}≠G, which shows it is not an abelian group. The centralizer of element 𝑟r is 𝐶𝐺(𝑟) =⟨𝑟⟩CG(r)=⟨r⟩, and the centralizer of element 𝑠s is 𝐶𝐺(𝑠) =⟨𝑠⟩CG(s)=⟨s⟩. In general, for all 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G, we always have ⟨𝑔⟩ ≤𝐶𝐺(𝑔)⟨g⟩≤CG(g). The conjugacy classes of group 𝐷6D6 are three in total: {𝑒},{𝑟,𝑟2},{𝑠,𝑠𝑟,𝑠𝑟2}{e},{r,r2},{s,sr,sr2}. It is easy to find that conjugate elements are all of the same order[^conjugate].

    Groups are divided into several conjugacy classes under conjugation. Therefore, we can write the class equation.

    Class Equation

    For group 𝐺G, let {K𝑖}𝑟𝑖=1{Ki}i=1r be all conjugacy classes with size greater than one, and let 𝑔𝑖gi be a representative of K𝑖Ki. Then

    |𝐺|=|𝑍(𝐺)|+𝑟∑𝑖=1[𝐺:𝐶𝐺(𝑔𝑖)].|G|=|Z(G)|+∑i=1r[G:CG(gi)].

    It can be used to analyze the structure of groups, for example, to prove the Sylow theorem below.

    Normalizers and Centralizers

    In fact, the power set of a group can also be the object of group actions. Here we focus mainly on the conjugation action of the group on its power set P(𝐺)P(G). Its permutation representation is as follows.

    𝜑:𝐺→𝑆𝑋𝑔↦𝜑𝑔:𝑋→𝑋𝑆↦𝑔𝑆𝑔−1={𝑔𝑠𝑔−1:𝑠∈𝑆}φ:G→SXg↦φg:X→XS↦gSg−1={gsg−1:s∈S}

    Under this conjugation action, we can similarly define conjugacy classes of subsets of the group. Its kernel is still the center of the group. Its stabilizer is called the normalizer.

    Normalizer

    For a group 𝐺G and its subset 𝑆 ⊆𝐺S⊆G, the normalizer of subset 𝑆S in group 𝐺G is 𝑁𝐺(𝑆) ={𝑔 ∈𝐺 :𝑔𝑆𝑔−1 =𝑆}NG(S)={g∈G:gSg−1=S}.

    The normalizer is the stabilizer of 𝑆S under conjugation, and is necessarily a subgroup of 𝐺G; the normalizer of 𝑆S is the largest subgroup among those subgroups that contain 𝑆S as a normal subgroup, which is also the origin of its name. Particularly, for singleton sets {𝑎}{a}, 𝑁𝐺({𝑎}) =𝐶𝐺(𝑎)NG({a})=CG(a).

    Centralizers can be similarly generalized to subsets.

    Centralizer

    For a group 𝐺G and its subset 𝑆 ⊆𝐺S⊆G, the centralizer of subset 𝑆S in group 𝐺G is 𝐶𝐺(𝑆) ={𝑔 ∈𝐺 :∀𝑠 ∈𝑆(𝑔𝑠𝑔−1 =𝑠)}CG(S)={g∈G:∀s∈S(gsg−1=s)}.

    The centralizer is actually the kernel of the conjugation action of 𝑁𝐺(𝑆)NG(S) on 𝑆S. Therefore, necessarily 𝐶𝐺(𝑆) ⊴𝑁𝐺(𝑆) ≤𝐺CG(S)⊴NG(S)≤G. So by the transitivity of subgroups, the centralizer is also a subgroup. Particularly, the center of the group 𝑍(𝐺) =𝐶𝐺(𝐺) ⊴𝑁𝐺(𝐺) =𝐺Z(G)=CG(G)⊴NG(G)=G is necessarily a normal subgroup.

    Sylow Theorems

    Further analyzing the conjugation actions of finite groups leads to Sylow theorems. It is a powerful tool for handling the structure of finite groups and can quickly obtain the structures of many small-order groups.

    𝑝p-Groups

    For a group 𝐺G, if there exists a prime number 𝑝p and a positive integer 𝛼α such that |𝐺| =𝑝𝛼|G|=pα, then it is called a 𝑝p-group.

    On the Definition of 𝑝p-Groups

    There is another definition for 𝑝p-groups, i.e., groups where all elements have orders that are powers of prime numbers. These two definitions are equivalent for finite groups; however, the second definition also applies to infinite groups. Additionally, regarding the definition of 𝑝p-groups, different literature may differ on whether to include {𝑒}{e} as a 𝑝p-group. Readers should distinguish when reading.

    𝑝p-Subgroups

    For a group 𝐺G and its subgroup 𝑃 ≤𝐺P≤G, if 𝑃P itself is a 𝑝p-group, then 𝑃P is called a 𝑝p-subgroup.

    Cauchy's Theorem

    If a prime number 𝑝p can divide the order of group 𝐺G, then there necessarily exists an element of order 𝑝p.

    Cauchy's theorem guarantees the existence of 𝑝p-subgroups. In fact, through more detailed analysis, we can get a stronger conclusion, i.e., the existence of Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups.

    Sylow 𝑝p-Subgroups

    For a group 𝐺G and its subgroup 𝑃 ≤𝐺P≤G, if |𝐺| =𝑝𝛼𝑚|G|=pαm, 𝑝 ⟂𝑚p⟂m and |𝑃| =𝑝𝛼|P|=pα, then 𝑃P is called a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup.

    That is, Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups are maximal 𝑝p-subgroups. Sylow theorems assert the existence of Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups, which provides a partial inverse to Lagrange's theorem.

    Sylow Theorems

    Let the order of finite group 𝐺G be |𝐺||G| expressed as 𝑝𝛼𝑚pαm, where 𝑝p is a prime and 𝑝 ∤𝑚p∤m. Then we have the following conclusions:

    1. There exists a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup;
    2. For a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑃P and a 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑄Q of group 𝐺G, there exists 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G such that 𝑄 ≤𝑔𝑃𝑔−1Q≤gPg−1 holds. In particular, all Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups are conjugate;
    3. The number 𝑛𝑝np of Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups in group 𝐺G satisfies 𝑛𝑝 ≡1(mod𝑝)np≡1(modp), 𝑛𝑝 ∣𝑚np∣m, and 𝑛𝑝 =[𝐺 :𝑁𝐺(𝑃)]np=[G:NG(P)], where 𝑃P is any Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup.
    Proof

    To prove the first part, perform induction on |𝐺||G|. Consider the class equation

    |𝐺|=|𝑍(𝐺)|+𝑟∑𝑖=1[𝐺:𝐶𝐺(𝑔𝑖)].|G|=|Z(G)|+∑i=1r[G:CG(gi)].

    If 𝑝 ∣|𝑍(𝐺)|p∣|Z(G)|, then we can take any subgroup 𝑁 ≤𝑍(𝐺)N≤Z(G) of order 𝑝p, which necessarily satisfies 𝑁 ⊴𝑍(𝐺) ⊴𝐺N⊴Z(G)⊴G, and therefore 𝐺/𝑁G/N is a smaller group. By the induction hypothesis, it has a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑃/𝑁P/N. Then the preimage under the natural homomorphism is a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup of the original group 𝐺G. So we only need to consider the case where 𝑝 ∤|𝑍(𝐺)|p∤|Z(G)|. At this time, we can take 𝑔𝑖 ∈𝐺gi∈G such that 𝑝 ∤[𝐺 :𝐶𝐺(𝑔𝑖)]p∤[G:CG(gi)]. Therefore, all powers of 𝑝p in |𝐺||G| appear in |𝐶𝐺(𝑔𝑖)||CG(gi)|. By the induction hypothesis again, 𝐶𝐺(𝑔𝑖)CG(gi) has a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑃P, which is a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup of the original group 𝐺G.

    To prove the second and third parts, let the conjugacy class of the Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑃P of group 𝐺G be S ={𝑔𝑃𝑔−1 :𝑔 ∈𝐺}S={gPg−1:g∈G}, and consider the conjugation action of group 𝐺G restricted to some 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑄Q on SS. This set SS can be divided into several orbits under this action. Let there be 𝑟r orbits in total, with representatives of each orbit being 𝑃𝑖Pi. Then we have the identity

    |S|=𝑟∑𝑖=1[𝑄:𝑄∩𝑁𝐺(𝑃𝑖)].|S|=∑i=1r[Q:Q∩NG(Pi)].

    Here, 𝑄 ∩𝑁𝐺(𝑃𝑖)Q∩NG(Pi) is the stabilizer of 𝑃𝑖Pi under the above group action. Let 𝐻 =𝑄 ∩𝑁𝐺(𝑃𝑖)H=Q∩NG(Pi). Obviously 𝐻 ≤𝑁𝐺(𝑃𝑖)H≤NG(Pi), so by the second isomorphism theorem, 𝑃𝑖𝐻/𝑃𝑖 ≅𝐻/(𝑃𝑖 ∩𝐻)PiH/Pi≅H/(Pi∩H). So, |𝑃𝑖𝐻| =|𝑃𝑖||𝐻|/|𝑃𝑖 ∩𝐻||PiH|=|Pi||H|/|Pi∩H|, and the right side is a power of 𝑝p. The left side must also be a power of 𝑝p, and we need |𝑃𝑖| ≤|𝑃𝑖𝐻||Pi|≤|PiH| to hold. However, 𝑃𝑖Pi is already the largest power of 𝑝p in subgroups of 𝐺G, so 𝑃𝑖 =𝑃𝑖𝐻Pi=PiH. Substituting into the isomorphism relation from earlier, we have 𝐻 =𝑃𝑖 ∩𝐻 =𝑄 ∩𝑃𝑖H=Pi∩H=Q∩Pi. Here we use the obvious relationship 𝑃𝑖 ≤𝑁𝐺(𝑃𝑖)Pi≤NG(Pi). Thus, we know that the stabilizer 𝑄 ∩𝑁𝐺(𝑃𝑖)Q∩NG(Pi) is actually 𝑄 ∩𝑃𝑖Q∩Pi. Therefore, the above formula can be written as

    |S|=𝑟∑𝑖=1[𝑄:𝑄∩𝑃𝑖].|S|=∑i=1r[Q:Q∩Pi].

    This equality holds for all 𝑝p-subgroups 𝑄Q.

    Naturally, the Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑃P is also a 𝑝p-subgroup. Substituting 𝑃P into the formula for 𝑄Q on the right side, there is only one term with size 1, and the others are all multiples of 𝑝p. Therefore, the size |S||S| of the conjugacy class of the Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑃P must be 1(mod𝑝)1(modp). At the same time, because this formula holds for any 𝑝p-subgroup 𝑄Q, there naturally exists 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G such that 𝑄 ≤𝑔𝑃𝑔−1Q≤gPg−1; otherwise, for all 𝑃𝑖Pi in the above equality, |𝑄 ∩𝑃𝑖| <|𝑄||Q∩Pi|<|Q|, which contradicts |S| ≡1(mod𝑝)|S|≡1(modp). If at this time we consider 𝑄Q as a Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup different from 𝑃P, then necessarily 𝑄 =𝑔𝑃𝑔−1Q=gPg−1 holds for some 𝑔 ∈𝐺g∈G, i.e., all Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups are conjugate. Therefore, the number 𝑛𝑝np of Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups is |S||S|, which necessarily satisfies 𝑛𝑝 ≡1(mod𝑝)np≡1(modp). Finally, note that 𝑛𝑝 =|S| =[𝐺 :𝑁𝐺(𝑃)]np=|S|=[G:NG(P)], and 𝑃 ≤𝑁𝐺(𝑃)P≤NG(P), so 𝑛𝑝 ∣𝑚np∣m. This completes the proof of the second and third parts of the theorem.

    Application: Up to Isomorphism, There Are Only 𝐶6C6 and 𝑆3S3 of Order 6

    Let 𝐺G be of order 6. Then by Sylow's theorem, it has a Sylow 22-subgroup, and its number satisfies 𝑛2 ≡1(mod2)n2≡1(mod2) and 𝑛2 ∣3n2∣3, so there are only two cases: 𝑛2 =1n2=1 or 𝑛2 =3n2=3. Similarly, we can prove that group 𝐺G has and only has one Sylow 33-subgroup, i.e., 𝑛3 =1n3=1.

    For the case 𝑛2 =1n2=1, we can find that group 𝐺G has a Sylow 22-subgroup, so it has an element of order 2; it also has a Sylow 33-subgroup, so it has two elements of order 3. Group 𝐺G also has an identity element. For the remaining elements, by Lagrange's theorem, their orders must divide 6. They cannot be new elements of order 2 or 3, otherwise they would create new Sylow 𝑝p-subgroups different from the previous ones. So the remaining elements are elements of order 6. The existence of an element with the same order as the group means that group 𝐺G is a cyclic group, so 𝐺 ≅𝐶6G≅C6.

    For the case 𝑛2 =3n2=3, group 𝐺G has three conjugate Sylow 33-subgroups. Consider the conjugation action of group 𝐺G on these three Sylow 33-subgroups. For any Sylow 33-subgroup 𝑃P, by Sylow's theorem, we have |𝑁𝐺(𝑃)| =2|NG(P)|=2; but we also have 𝑃 ≤𝑁𝐺(𝑃)P≤NG(P), so 𝑃 =𝑁𝐺(𝑃)P=NG(P). Therefore, the intersection of the normalizers of these three Sylow 33-subgroups, i.e., the kernel of this conjugation action, is trivial. So this action is faithful, and it embeds 𝐺G into the permutation group 𝑆3S3 on these three Sylow 33-subgroups. However, because |𝐺| =|𝑆3||G|=|S3|, necessarily 𝐺 ≅𝑆3G≅S3.

    Finitely Generated Abelian Groups

    After mastering the basic tools for analyzing group structure, we now focus on the structure of a class of groups.

    In the overview, it was mentioned that abelian groups have simpler structures because elements can commute. Among these, particularly simple are those abelian groups that can be generated from finitely many elements.

    Finitely Generated

    If a group 𝐺G has a finite generating set, then group 𝐺G is called finitely generated.

    The classification theorem in this section shows that finitely generated abelian groups can be seen as simple combinations of finitely many cyclic groups. The groups involved in competitive programming are mostly finite groups. Finite abelian groups are necessarily finitely generated, so this conclusion always applies to them.

    Direct Product

    The analysis of groups above mainly focused on how to decompose groups into smaller groups; conversely, we can naturally discuss how to combine two groups into a larger group. Among all possible combination methods, the direct product of groups is the simplest.

    The basic idea of the direct product of groups is: given two groups 𝐺G and 𝐻H, consider their Cartesian product 𝐺 ×𝐻G×H, where the operation on the pair (𝑔,ℎ)(g,h) is to perform operations on each component separately, with the components not affecting each other. The result is obviously a larger group, and the original two groups can be trivially embedded into the new group.

    Direct Product

    The direct product of groups (𝐺, ⋅𝐺)(G,⋅G) and (𝐻, ⋅𝐻)(H,⋅H) is the group (𝐺 ×𝐻, ⋅)(G×H,⋅), where the binary operation ⋅ :(𝐺 ×𝐻) ×(𝐺 ×𝐻) →𝐺 ×𝐻⋅:(G×H)×(G×H)→G×H is defined as (𝑔1,ℎ1) ⋅(𝑔2,ℎ2) =(𝑔1 ⋅𝐺𝑔2,ℎ1 ⋅𝐻ℎ2)(g1,h1)⋅(g2,h2)=(g1⋅Gg2,h1⋅Hh2). The direct product of groups 𝐺G and 𝐻H is denoted 𝐺 ×𝐻G×H.

    For the direct product 𝐺 ×𝐻G×H, we trivially have embedding maps 𝑔 ↦(𝑔,𝑒𝐻)g↦(g,eH) and ℎ ↦(𝑒𝐺,ℎ)h↦(eG,h). Conversely, the mapping (𝑔,ℎ) ↦𝑔(g,h)↦g and the mapping (𝑔,ℎ) ↦ℎ(g,h)↦h are group homomorphisms, and their kernels are respectively {𝑒𝐺} ×𝐻{eG}×H and 𝐺 ×{𝑒𝐻}G×{eH}. These two kernels are exactly the images of the above embedding mappings, and their intersection is trivial, i.e., {(𝑒𝐺,𝑒𝐻)}{(eG,eH)}. Therefore, in the direct product 𝐺 ×𝐻G×H, there are two subgroups, both normal subgroups, their intersection is trivial, and their product is the direct product 𝐺 ×𝐻G×H itself.

    This analysis actually gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a group to be written as the direct product of its two subgroups.

    Theorem

    For a group 𝐺G and its subgroups 𝐻1,𝐻2 ≤𝐺H1,H2≤G, 𝐺 ≅𝐻1 ×𝐻2G≅H1×H2 if and only if 𝐻1,𝐻2 ⊴𝐺H1,H2⊴G, 𝐻1 ∩𝐻2 ={𝑒}H1∩H2={e}, and 𝐺 =𝐻1𝐻2G=H1H2.

    Proof

    The necessity of these conditions has been discussed in the main text. Here we prove their sufficiency. Consider the mapping 𝜑 :𝐺 →𝐻1 ×𝐻2φ:G→H1×H2 satisfying ℎ1ℎ2 ↦(ℎ1,ℎ2)h1h2↦(h1,h2). The mapping 𝜑φ is well-defined because for any ℎ1,𝑘1 ∈𝐻1h1,k1∈H1 and ℎ2,𝑘2 ∈𝐻2h2,k2∈H2, satisfying ℎ1ℎ2 =𝑘1𝑘2h1h2=k1k2 implies ℎ1 =𝑘1h1=k1 and ℎ2 =𝑘2h2=k2; this is because 𝑘−11ℎ1 =𝑘2ℎ−12 ∈𝐻1 ∩𝐻2 ={𝑒}k1−1h1=k2h2−1∈H1∩H2={e}. To show that 𝜑φ is a group homomorphism, we need to show (ℎ1ℎ2)(𝑘1𝑘2) =ℎ1𝑘1ℎ2𝑘2(h1h2)(k1k2)=h1k1h2k2, which is equivalent to 𝑘1k1 and ℎ2h2 being commutative, i.e., 𝑘1ℎ2𝑘−11ℎ−12 =𝑒k1h2k1−1h2−1=e. To prove this relationship, just note that 𝑘1ℎ2𝑘−11ℎ−12 =(𝑘1ℎ2𝑘−11)ℎ−12 ∈(𝑘1𝐻2𝑘−11)𝐻2 =𝐻2k1h2k1−1h2−1=(k1h2k1−1)h2−1∈(k1H2k1−1)H2=H2, and similarly 𝑘1(ℎ2𝑘−11ℎ−12) ∈𝐻1k1(h2k1−1h2−1)∈H1, so 𝑘1ℎ2𝑘−11ℎ−12 ∈𝐻1 ∩𝐻2 ={𝑒}k1h2k1−1h2−1∈H1∩H2={e}. These prove that 𝜑φ is a group homomorphism. It is obviously a bijection, so it is an isomorphism, i.e., 𝐺 ≅𝐻1 ×𝐻2G≅H1×H2.

    In direct products, elements of the two direct product factors must commute because ℎ𝑔 =(𝑒𝐺,ℎ)(𝑔,𝑒𝐻) =(𝑔,ℎ) =𝑔ℎhg=(eG,h)(g,eH)=(g,h)=gh. So if both direct product factors are abelian, the direct product is necessarily abelian.

    Not all groups can be written as the direct product of two non-trivial subgroups.

    Example: Spatial Symmetry Group 𝐷6D6 of Equilateral Triangle (continued)

    For example, group 𝐷6 =⟨𝑟,𝑠⟩D6=⟨r,s⟩ is not isomorphic to ⟨𝑟⟩ ×⟨𝑠⟩⟨r⟩×⟨s⟩, because the direct product of the two cyclic groups must be abelian.

    The following classification theorem shows that finitely generated abelian groups can all be written as direct products of finitely many cyclic groups.

    Classification Theorem

    For finitely generated abelian groups, there is the following classification theorem. It is called the Fundamental Theorem of Finitely Generated Abelian Groups.

    Fundamental Theorem of Finitely Generated Abelian Groups

    For a finitely generated abelian group 𝐺G, there exist integers 𝑟 ≥0r≥0 and 𝑛1,⋯,𝑛𝑠 ≥2n1,⋯,ns≥2 such that

    𝐺≅𝐶𝑟∞×𝐶𝑛1×⋯×𝐶𝑛𝑠.G≅C∞r×Cn1×⋯×Cns.

    In particular, 𝑟r is uniquely determined and is called the rank of group 𝐺G. Moreover,

    • We can choose integers 𝑛1,⋯,𝑛𝑠n1,⋯,ns such that 𝑛1 ≥2, 𝑛1|𝑛2, ⋯, 𝑛𝑠−1|𝑛𝑠n1≥2, n1|n2, ⋯, ns−1|ns. At this time, integers 𝑛1,⋯,𝑛𝑠n1,⋯,ns are uniquely determined, and the factor 𝐶𝑛𝑖Cni is called the invariant factor of group 𝐺G;
    • We can also choose integers 𝑛1,⋯,𝑛𝑠n1,⋯,ns to all be powers of primes. At this time, these prime powers are also uniquely determined, and the factor 𝐶𝑛𝑖Cni is called the elementary divisor of group 𝐺G.

    The theorem first asserts that finitely generated abelian groups are necessarily direct products of finitely many cyclic groups.

    Proof

    Here we give a proof with simple form; a more profound proof should refer to the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over principal ideal domains[^module-pid]. In the proof, for writing convenience, we use additive notation instead of the general multiplicative notation in groups. At this time, 00 represents the identity element, and 𝑚𝑥mx represents the 𝑚m-th power of 𝑥x.

    Let 𝐺G be minimally generated by 𝑘k elements. The proof needs to be done by induction on 𝑘k. When 𝑘 =1k=1, the conclusion is trivial. When 𝑘 >1k>1, take the smallest order among generators ⟨𝑥1,𝑥2,⋯,𝑥𝑘⟩⟨x1,x2,⋯,xk⟩ that generates 𝐺G. Next we want to show 𝐺 =⟨𝑥1⟩ ×⟨𝑥2,⋯,𝑥𝑘⟩G=⟨x1⟩×⟨x2,⋯,xk⟩. The latter can be decomposed into the direct product of 𝑘 −1k−1 cyclic groups by the induction hypothesis, so the induction step is proven.

    According to the characterization of direct products, if the direct product decomposition does not hold, there necessarily exists a relationship 𝑚1𝑥1 +𝑚2𝑥2 +⋯ +𝑚𝑘𝑥𝑘 =0m1x1+m2x2+⋯+mkxk=0, and 𝑚1𝑥1 ≠0m1x1≠0. For negative coefficients 𝑚𝑖mi, we can replace 𝑥𝑖xi with its inverse −𝑥𝑖−xi. Then all coefficients 𝑚𝑖mi can be taken as non-negative integers. Moreover, we can take 0 <𝑚1 <|𝑥1|0<m1<|x1|. If we further take 𝑑 =gcd(𝑚1,𝑚2,⋯,𝑚𝑘)d=gcd(m1,m2,⋯,mk) and 𝑐𝑖 =𝑚𝑖/𝑑ci=mi/d, then there necessarily exists 𝑦1 =𝑐1𝑥1 +𝑐2𝑥2 +⋯ +𝑐𝑘𝑥𝑘y1=c1x1+c2x2+⋯+ckxk satisfying 𝑑𝑦1 =0dy1=0, so |𝑦1| ≤𝑑 ≤𝑚1 <|𝑥1||y1|≤d≤m1<|x1|, i.e., 𝑦1y1 is an element of smaller order than 𝑥1x1.

    Next we prove that 𝑦1y1 can be expanded into a set of generators of 𝐺G. That is, there exist elements 𝑦2,⋯,𝑦𝑘 ∈𝐺y2,⋯,yk∈G such that 𝐺 =⟨𝑦1,𝑦2,⋯,𝑦𝑘⟩G=⟨y1,y2,⋯,yk⟩. The only known condition is that 𝑦1y1 itself can be written as 𝑐1𝑥1 +𝑐2𝑥2 +⋯ +𝑐𝑘𝑥𝑘c1x1+c2x2+⋯+ckxk, where the coefficients 𝑐𝑖ci are all natural numbers and their greatest common divisor is 1. Assuming the coefficients are arranged in (non-strict) descending order, 𝑦1y1 can also be written as (𝑐1 −𝑐2)𝑥1 +𝑐2(𝑥1 +𝑥2) +⋯ +𝑐𝑘𝑥𝑘(c1−c2)x1+c2(x1+x2)+⋯+ckxk. If 𝑐2 =0c2=0, then necessarily 𝑐1 =1c1=1, and the conclusion is trivial; otherwise, the sum of coefficients strictly decreases.
